 Mr. Boyd, with his WCVB co-anchor Susan Wornick and meteorologist David Brown. WCVB 
 Jim Boyd was only 19 when he reached a crossroads. He had started college three years earlier, only to be asked to leave because his grades were poor, a story he later recounted as getting a letter from the “can’t people,” as in: “Jim, you can’t come back.” 
 Realizing he had to turn his life around, Mr. Boyd began his broadcasting career on the lowest rung, the mailroom of National Educational Television in New York City. One day he found himself in a production studio “and I realized at that point that there was something there I found very attractive,” he said at a 2012 seniors conference in Quincy . “This is a television studio. This is how they put television programs on the air.” 
 Rising steadily, he traveled the world as an NET producer and then moved to Boston, where for years he was a top-rated anchor of morning and midday newscasts on WCVB-TV, Channel 5. 
 Get Starting Point A guide through the most important stories of the morning, delivered Monday through Friday. Enter Email Sign Up “It all turned out extraordinarily well for me,” he told a Concord gathering in 2013 . “I realized good things happen to good people even if they had made a mistake or two.” 
 Mr. Boyd, who was inducted into the Massachusetts Broadcasters Hall of Fame in 2012 and finished his long-set-aside bachelor’s degree the following year, died Tuesday. He was 84, had lived in Needham for many years, and his health had been failing. 
 During his nearly four-decade WCVB career, Mr. Boyd made numerous visits to schools and to community groups such as the YMCA in Roxbury and the Youth Enrichment Services to speak with and inspire children and youths. 
 He also routinely paused to converse with anyone who recognized him on the streets, impressing strangers with his gentlemanly presence — a trait not associated with all who hold high-pressure media jobs. 
 “Anybody who came up to talk with him, he would talk with them,” said his wife, Linda Polach. “He met presidents and lawn workers, and speakers of the house and garbage collectors. He was the same with everybody. He respected everyone as an equal.” 
 He embodied the same courteous quality on camera as well. Susan Wornick, his longtime Channel 5 co-anchor , said one of the first questions viewers always asked her was: “Is Jim as nice as he seems?” 
 The answer was yes. “Truly, he had that impact on people,” she recalled. 
 Emily Rooney, who had worked with Mr. Boyd and Wornick as news director at Channel 5 , recalled that Mr. Boyd was the kind of employee “every manager would like to clone — loyal, dedicated, didn’t call in sick, and never complained about an assignment.” 
 Rooney, who went on to host “Beat the Press” on GBH-TV for many years, added that “he was also movie-star handsome and had that elusive journalistic credibility.” 
 Channel 5 anchor Jim Boyd at a Healthy Kids Fair in 1997. Bill Brett/Globe Staff Mr. Boyd connected with colleagues and competitors as readily as he did with WCVB’s viewers. 
 “Jim was the consummate hard-working reporter and more importantly he was a great guy,” said the Rev. Liz Walker, a retired pastor of Roxbury Presbyterian Church and former WBZ-TV anchor. 
 “I remember when I first came to Boston, I found most television folks to be a little distant and aloof,” said Walker who was the first woman of color to anchor a Boston TV news show . “Jim was friendly, kind, knowledgeable, welcoming, and helpful. He was a real gentleman on and off camera.” 
 Mr. Boyd was almost always unflappable at the anchor desk, though once in a while his co-anchor, Wornick, would say something that would stop him short. 
 “He was kind of the straight man in our team,” Wornick said, adding with a chuckle that their inside joke was that “he lived in constant fear that I’d say something that would put us out of a job.” 
 On one occasion, Rooney recalled, “Wornick said about a python living under a home in Florida. Jim said, ‘Looks like trouble to me.’ Wornick said, ‘Looks like shoes and a bag to me.’” 
 Born in New York City on March 26, 1942, Mr. Boyd grew up in Harlem, a son of Edmonia Coleman Boyd, a secretary and receptionist, and Leroy Homer Boyd, a mail carrier. Mr. Boyd’s paternal grandfather, Arthur Boyd, had performed as a violinist with the accomplished Negro String Quartet. 
 By his own description, Mr. Boyd wasn’t a devoted student. 
 Instead of classrooms, “I liked to play sports,” he recalled in a WCVB interview . “I liked to pretty much do anything other than go to school and sit in class and come home and do homework.” 
 Mr. Boyd was 16 when he enrolled at Long Island University in New York, only to be told to leave three years later. 
 While working for National Educational Television, he took classes at Fairleigh Dickinson University in Teaneck, N.J. But work assignments, several overseas, kept forcing him to decide which educational experiences were more worthwhile: his work or his studies. 
 “There were opportunities for me to go to Paris or go to class. I went to Paris. The opportunity to go to Cairo or go to class. I went to Cairo,” he said at the 2012 seniors conference in Quincy. 
 A Ford Foundation grant provided the opportunity for a sojourn in Boston honing his production skills at what was then WGBH-TV, where he contributed to early broadcasts of the program “Say Brother,” later renamed “Basic Black.” 
 After more time at NET in New York City, he returned to Boston in the early 1970s to work at WCVB as a general assignment reporter before becoming a weekend anchor, and then a morning and midday anchor. 
 Before retiring at the end of 2008, he finished his Channel 5 tenure as a special correspondent and field reporter. 
 Mr. Boyd, whose first marriage ended in divorce, married Polach, then a Channel 5 executive producer, in 1984 . 
 In a home of two broadcast news professionals, “there’s a lot of channel flicking” to keep tabs on the competition, he said in a 1991 Boston Globe interview. 
 After leaving WCVB, Mr. Boyd took courses at the University of Massachusetts Boston. 
 Then he finished a bachelor’s degree in sociology through Tufts University’s Resumed Education for Adult Learning program, graduating in 2013 at the age of 71 — 55 years after finishing high school. 
 “It’s been really fascinating to see him immerse himself into something so different from what he did for a living, and enjoy something that, quite honestly, a lot of people take for granted,” Polach told the Globe then . “To see someone so intellectually engaged is wonderful. It’s like somebody opened up a new world for him.” 
 Mr. Boyd leaves his wife and his three daughters, Erica Jacob, Alyssa Pannozzi, and Olivia; and two grandchildren. 
 A celebration of life will be announced. 
 Known for the active role he took in helping raise his two daughters with Polach, Mr. Boyd began his days at 2:30 a.m. and headed into the Channel 5 newsroom to prepare the morning newscast. 
 After the midday news concluded, he quickly returned to Needham to be there when his daughters got home from school, or to bring them to activities and coach their sports teams. 
 “You do the things that are important, the things that have meaning to me and the kids,” Mr. Boyd told the Globe in 1997. “I wish I could do more.” 
 And though he was recognizable throughout Greater Boston because of his work, “he did not care about the limelight,” Wornick said. “He cared about the issues, and he cared about his family, first and foremost.”
